Can you show a screen shot (redact your email address)? That might clarify what you mean by "duplicating".

Do you have Thunderbird set to automatically show remote content? This option is found at <Settings | Privacy & Security | Mail Content | Allow remote content in messages>?

Does the email have a "Show in browser" option? How does the message look in a browser?

Without seeing the actual source code of the email my guesses are...

Thunderbird can only render the content of what's actually in the message, and unfortunately, many emails contain invalid web (HTML) code or formatting. Some readers are more strict or lax than others at glossing over those errors - maybe Thunderbird is one of strict ones.

Many or most HTML emails also include a plain-text version, and code in the email separates the two versions. It could be that the separator is incorrect and Thunderbird can't distinguish between the two and so displays them as one.

This is all a long-winded way to say that there may not be anything you can do. But try switching the message view between "Original HTML", "Plain HTML" and "Plain Text" and see if you like the appearance better. This setting is found at menu option <View | Message body as>. If the menu is hidden, press <Alt> or <F10> to reveal it.

content:
When someone sends an email to you a few things could happen, assuming yours is a POP account...

Scenario 1: It's received by your email provider (Earthlink?) and placed in your Inbox on the mail server out there on the Internet. Thunderbird on your local computer will check the server Inbox, and ONLY the Inbox, and if it finds new messages there, it will download them to your local computer and delete them from the server, leaving the only copy on your computer. That copy will be found in Thunderbird's Inbox, or possibly in one of its other folders. You should check all local folders (you can use Thunderbird's Search features to do this more easily.)

Scenario 2: It's received by your email provider (Earthlink?), who decides it's spam, and moves the message to their Spam folder. Since Thunderbird checks ONLY the server's Inbox for new messages, not its spam folder, Thunderbird will not know it's there and won't download it. The only way to see the message is to go to Earthlink's web mail.

Scenario 3: The sender sends the message, but there's a problem delivering it to Earthlink. The problem might not necessarily be Earthlink's - there are many points of possible failure between sender and recipient. What's supposed to happen is that the sender's mail server will keep trying to deliver it for up to several days or more, and if it keeps failing, the sender should eventually receive a non-delivery notice, but it may not happen right away.

Scenario 4: Earthlink, or someone else in the chain could be misconfigured or malfunctioning and silently rejecting the message. This isn't supposed to happen... but it sometimes does.


What this all means is that if you are receiving all other email except from this one sender, and you have searched all your local Thunderbird folders, and have checked all folders in your Earthlink web mail, then I can confidently say the message was never received.

I don't think this is a Thunderbird issue. Your next step would probably be to contact Earthlink's tech support.

content:
You can import Thunderbird's address book into Cardbook this way:

- Right-click anywhere in Cardbook's address book list pane and from the context menu choose "New Address Book", then "Import Thunderbird's standard address books", then follow the prompts.


You can also import contacts from a VCF, CSV, or other file this way:

content:
Here is some information supplied by the email account provider:

When creating a new folder, the server shows error: "{imaps} Bad flag in APPEND command: Nonjunk"

The error is clear — the IMAP server is rejecting the APPEND command because Thunderbird is sending two junk-related flags simultaneously:

$notjunk — a valid IMAP keyword flag NonJunk — a non-standard flag (no backslash prefix) that the server doesn't accept

This is a Thunderbird-side behavior — it's sending both $notjunk and NonJunk together when moving messages to newly created folders, and the server's IMAP parser rejects NonJunk as invalid.

content:
The answer is, "No." Yahoo, Gmail, and many other email providers authenticate you using OAuth2. What happens is when Thunderbird first contacts Yahoo to send or receive email, it will ask for your Yahoo password. It will then set what's known as a "token" in your Saved Passwords, which appears as a seemingly-arbitrary string of characters and is NOT your actual password. The token indicates that you have been verified as you on that particular machine with your correct password. This is considered to be far more secure than the old plain password authentication method.

According to this article, AT&T also uses OAuth, but I have no personal experience with it:

https://www.att.com/support/article/email-support/KM1240462/

Here's an article that describes OAuth2 in good detail:

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/tb-oauth

creator: jfgies

content:
No. You use your regular password everywhere, both with webmail AND in Thunderbird, when prompted. The difference is that Thunderbird won't store your password on your computer, but instead it will store a record (the token) of having authenticated you. Remember that the token is not a password, per se, and you will never need to know it.

But if you DO decide to change your password on AT&T or Yahoo, you may need to delete the tokens saved in Thunderbird's Saved Passwords, after which you will be prompted to authenticate anew... with your new password. Once you're authenticated, a brand new token will be set.

content:
There are at least two factors here.

- There is no version of Thunderbird that runs on iOS, so you will need to find another email app that can do IMAP and SMTP mail, which are the standard Internet email protocols. I don't use Apple products, so I can't recommend one, but I know they're out there. When you find one, set it up to use IMAP, not' 'POP3.

- The email program on your PC (Thunderbird, I presume) should also be set up as an IMAP account, not POP3.

If all devices that talk to your email server are using IMAP, they will all synchronize with each other and all will show the same emails. If any one of them is using POP3, they will likely get out of sync and create confusion.


The article below discusses IMAP and how it is an advantage in a situation like yours:

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/imap-synchronization

content:
So, you want to use the account you just set up with the email address you indicated, but you want the messages you send to have a different "friendly" name than what you originally used, right? That can be changed to anything you like at any time. Go to <Account Settings | (the account in question) | Default Identity | Your Name> - change that to whatever you want. This is your default Identity and by default all new messages will show that name.

You can also set up multiple identities that can have various other friendly names, and you can choose from them when you create a message. Here's an article that goes into detail about that feature:

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/using-identities

You can also edit the "From" name on the fly when you're in the message creation window by choosing "Custom From Address" from the From drop-down list.

content:
There's no built-in way to do that, and it wouldn't be a good idea for most people, since the filters run in the order they're listed, and if the order is changed they may not produce the desired results.

If you're handy with a text editor and careful, a plain-text filters rule files, "msgFilterRules.dat" can be found in your Profile, a separate one for each email account. This could be edited with a text editor and the blocks of rules could be moved around. This probably wouldn't be any faster than using the Thunderbird interface unless you used some fancy macros or scripting in the editor.

content:
You do get an error for mail.mediacombb.net. However, your server settings use imap.mediacombb.net, and smtp.mediacombb.net respectively. So obviously there is a mismatch, which may be part of the problem. I don't know which server name is correct, you'll have to check with MC.

Beyond that, the certificate for imap.mediacombb.net is a mess. It uses outdated TLS versions, and is vulnerable to certain attacks. See https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/analyze.html?d=mail.mediacombb.net

Thunderbird does not accept TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 by default. Starting with Thunderbird version 78, support for TLS 1.0 and 1.1 was deprecated and disabled for security reasons, making TLS 1.2 the minimum required version.

If I were you I'd find a new email provider who know what they are doing.

MC tech informed me that M$ Outlook is more friendly than TB.

That somehow fits into the picture. As opposed to Outlook, Thunderbird is more strict in enforcing security. Outlook prioritizes convenience over security, so it potentially puts you at risk. And so does MC it seems.

What version of Thunderbird? The answer may be slightly different depending on which.

- For versions prior to 15x.x, you need to make sure that Cookies are allowed (see <Settings | Privacy & Security | Web Content | Accept cookies from sites>. content:
Thunderbird does not have "an account" as is the case with many mail clients, it has incoming accounts and outgoing accounts and they are linked via the identity information on the incoming account (there is also no limit on the number of distinct identities you can have on and incoming account.)

I therefore really do not follow your line of thought. There is no limit to the number of SMTP servers that can be configured and each can have it's own used name and password. The SMTP to be used with an identity is set in the account settings for the incoming account on the identity pane (the one above server settings)

Check the outgoing server(SMTP) entry in account settings for configured outgoing servers and add whatever you need.

Open Settings: Right-click on your account name in the left sidebar and select Settings (or click the Gear icon at the bottom left).


To solve this issue , follow this


To open settings, right-click your account name and choose Settings. You can also click the three-line menu or gear icon.

Delete account: Look for old HostGator addresses in the list, select the account, and remove it.

Remove SMTP server: Scroll down in the account settings, click Outgoing Server (SMTP), select the HostGator server, and click Remove.

Clean up profile (optional): If the issue persists, close Thunderbird. Press Windows Key + R, type thunderbird.exe -p, and hit Enter. Create a new profile or delete old/corrupted ones here.

Old passwords, tokens, and security keys conflict with this server. These duplicates occur because newer data should already exist, confusing Thunderbird. Disconnect temporarily until fixed. As stated above, remove HostGator, update credentials, and backup old HostGator data (Synced data will be erased permanently.) to a separate folder before deciding to delete it


Hopefully, these steps solved part of your issue. HostGator is removed, so you can start Thunderbird without it. I hope they don't come back, but if they do, just send us another message

After deleting those accounts, getting the new version of Thunderbird will help. Cleaning the PC with CCleaner and reinstalling your software is a good choice. After that you can use both email programs together again if you like

content: With IMAP all mail is managed on the server. The IMAP client, i.e. Thunderbird, is just like a mirror of what's on the server. The IMAP server did delete your restored local backup, because it knew nothing about it. This isn't a bug, it's just how IMAP works. Therefore you need to restore the backup to your Local Folders account. Then you can upload the restored messages to the IMAP server. Email servers are not made for mass transactions and may limit the amount of data and/or no. of messages being transferred. So copy your messages to the server in smaller badges, and no all at once.

Can you please clarify for my understanding how to 'restore the backup to my Local Folders'?

After restoring your backup, and while Thunderbird is still in offline mode, copy the restored message from your IMAP account to your Local Folders account.

Second, how to upload to the IMAP server? I assume that would be done via the web GUI on yahoo.com?

If you do have some sort of folder hierarchy, manually re-create it on the server in case it doesn't exist. This part can also be done via webmail. Then, in Thunderbird, select the messages to be transferred to the server - right-click a selected message - Copy To Select your IMAP account, and the desired destination folder on the server.

As stated before, do the copy your messages in smaller batches, and for each folder. Don't copy everything at once.

content:
If yours was a POP account, messages in the Archive folders are local to your computer, though still listed among the Spectrum folders. They will be accessible, but I recommend that you move them all to the Local Folders pseudo-account. That way you can eventually delete Spectrum from your accounts in Thunderbird and your archives will be out of the way and safe and accessible.

If yours was an IMAP account, and your Spectrum account is still active, it's possible that when they shut you off (or you shut them off) the Archive folder(s) might become inaccessible. To avoid this, copy anything you want to keep into Local Folders. Then, when you're ready, you can delete the Spectrum account from Thunderbird.

In other words, anything in the Local Folders hierarchy is on your computer and unaffected with any other on-line email account.

Please consider making regular backups of your Thunderbird profile. That include all your carefully archived local messages.
